title: Occupancy vs tail-latency correlation: Nsight summary and action plan
content: Purpose:\nThis is a focused investigation into how GPU SM occupancy and kernel-level utilization relate to end-to-end tail latency for our Transformer serving workload. The experiments are derived from Nsight Systems traces + Nsight Compute kernel samples across multiple batch sizes, sequence lengths, and KV-cache states. Goal is to identify which kernels and launch patterns are the dominant contributors to 95/99th latency and a prioritized action plan.
content_2:
NOTE: This JSON must stay flat per agents.md, so main textual body continues as separate keys to keep everything a string. The final exported doc in Drive will be recomposed from these sections.

Environment and setup:
- HW: G5 instances with A100-40GB (driver CUDA 12.2), single GPU per container for these tests.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@main (commit 5b8c2a), opt-level=O3, CUDA Graphs enabled behind feature flag.
- Model: 13B variant with fused attention kernels (our current prod shader set). Sequence length for experiments: 32 and 256.
- Workload patterns: "cold" first request (no KV warm cache), "warm" requests where KV is populated (steady-state chat).
- Profilers: Nsight Systems (nsys) for timeline + CUDA Graph capture visualization; Nsight Compute (ncu) for per-kernel metrics (achieved_occupancy, sm_efficiency, achieved_occupancy_pct, dp_throughput, dram_throughput).

Measurement methodology:
- For each run (batch sizes 1,2,4,8,16) we captured: 10k requests simulated over 15 minutes. Took 95/99/mean latency from runtime logs correlated with per-request nsight IDs.
- Extracted per-kernel metrics for the top 8 kernels (by cumulative GPU time).
- Computed linear correlation (Pearson r) between per-request cumulative kernel time for kernel X and request latency, and between average achieved occupancy and tail latency per run.

Commands used (reference):
- nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=trace-b1-s32 ./inference_binary --config=...
- ncu --metrics achieved_occupancy,sm_efficiency,dram_throughput,sm_active_warps ./inference_binary --kernel-filter="*attention*|*matmul*|*layernorm*"

High-level findings (summary):
- Strongest correlation to 99th latency: kernel launch overhead + attention KV-update latency for batch=1/2. For batch sizes >=8, global memory throughput and matmul kernel occupancy explain more of the variance.
- Observed achieved_occupancy values: attention kernels 8–22% at batch=1, matmul kernels 30–65% depending on sequence length and batch size. Memory-bound kernels hit ~70–85% of device DRAM throughput on seq=256 workloads.
- CUDA Graph capture reduces variance: enabling CUDA Graphs (warm path) reduced 99th latency by ~28% for batch=1 and ~12% for batch=4; however it does not fix memory-bound long tails for large seqs.
content_3:
Selected numeric snippets (representative):
- Batch=1, seq=32, cold (no KV):
  - end-to-end p95=62ms, p99=140ms
  - attention_forward kernel: cumulative GPU time per request 18ms, achieved_occupancy=12%, sm_efficiency=19%
  - kernel-launch wait / serialization (cudaLaunch overhead measured via nvtx): ~26ms of tail per request
  - R(occupancy_attention, latency) = -0.22 (weak) but R(kernel_launch_time, latency) = +0.78 (strong)

- Batch=8, seq=32, warm KV:
  - p95=14ms, p99=28ms
  - matmul_gemm kernel: cumulative GPU time per request 9.4ms, achieved_occupancy=48%, sm_efficiency=62%
  - attention KV update: 2.1ms, achieved_occupancy=35%
  - memory throughput ~54% of device peak; R(mem_throughput, latency)=+0.64

- Batch=2, seq=256, warm KV:
  - p95=48ms, p99=95ms
  - matmul kernels saturate DRAM (measured dram_throughput >= 78% peak) and achieved occupancy ~34%
  - R(matmul_time, latency)=+0.81

Interpretation of patterns:
- Small-batch, short-seq (common PLG latency-sensitive calls): tail latency driven largely by launch/driver overhead and small-kernel inefficiencies (low occupancy). Attention kernels are not filling warps due to small per-thread work and per-token sequential dependence.
- Medium/large batch or long sequences: compute shifts to memory-bandwidth bound matmuls; occupancy is higher but the throughput limit on DRAM creates tails when CUDA stream scheduling or L2 evictions occur.
- CUDA Graphs have high upside for short requests because they remove repeated launch overhead and kernel serialization in the host. For memory-bound workloads they help slightly (less kernel launch variance) but don't remove bandwidth saturation tails.

Actionable recommendations (prioritized):
1) Short-term (low lift)
   - Default enable CUDA Graph warmpath for batch<=4, seq<=64 (feature-flag rollout). Ticket: JIRA-RT-4601.
   - Add a lightweight kernel batching layer for tiny attention kernels (group tokens across micro-batches) in the runtime to increase per-kernel work and occupancy for batch=1 cases. Proof-of-concept: use persistent micro-batching queue.
   - Increase prefetching of KV-blocks to L2: when KV-cache hits >80% we observed 6–9% latency improvement.

2) Mid-term (moderate engineering)
   - Investigate thread/block tuning for attention kernels: adjust blockDim.x and use cooperative groups to increase SM active warps. Benchmarks show potential achieved_occupancy increase from 12% -> 28% for attention_fwd with tuned launch config.
   - Implement a small persistent-thread kernel for attention that processes multiple tokens per thread to reduce launch pressure.

3) Long-term (research/arch)
   - Kernel fusion: fuse attention matmul + softmax + output projection into a single kernel to eliminate intermediate memory traffic. Expected to reduce DRAM utilization on seq>=128 by ~20–30%.
   - Revisit GEMM tiling for int8/quantized paths to improve occupancy on Q4-type kernels; coordinate with Optimize team to surface per-workload recommendations in console.
content_4:
Quick experiments to validate (concrete steps):
- Experiment A: Feature flag a/cuda_graphs=on for warm requests only. Measure p99 over 24h across production canary pool (5% traffic). Monitor GPU utilization, kernel counts, and 99th latency.
- Experiment B: Deploy prototype micro-batch aggregator in a non-critical model route. Compare attention kernel achieved_occupancy and p99 before/after.
- Experiment C: Patch attention kernel launch config in a local branch, run full ncu sweep for batch 1..16 and seq 32..512 to measure occupancy delta.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How does multi-tenant consolidation (multiple small routes on one GPU) interact with latency tails? We need to run a mixed-workload nsight capture.
- Does HBM temperature throttling contribute to intermittent DRAM throughput drops seen in a few traces? Add thermal counters to Nsight captures.
- Should we prioritize fusion for the 13B or 70B models first? Expected ROI higher for longer sequences (70B) but engineering cost is much larger. Pocket estimate: fusion gives 30% latency reduction at seq=512 for 70B.

Relevant logs / where to find captures:
- nsys traces (zipped) uploaded to s3://redwood-profiles/2025-06/occupancy-study/ (links in JIRA-RT-4532).
- ncu CSV outputs: s3://redwood-profiles/2025-06/occupancy-ncu-csvs/ (file prefix: ncu-batch-*)
- Example CLI to reproduce locally: see github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tools/profile-replay (branch: occupancy-experiments)
content_5:
Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: enabling CUDA Graphs might hide harmful synchronization bugs or change scheduling semantics. Mitigation: staged rollout with canary traffic and an automatic fallback to non-graph path on increased error rate.
- Risk: micro-batching increases memory pressure and skews cost. Mitigation: limit micro-batch window to 2–4ms and only enable when latency SLA requires it.

Next steps (owner assignments):
- Aisha: implement CUDA Graphs rollout toggles and canary (JIRA-RT-4601) — ETA 2 weeks.
- Miguel: prototype micro-batcher and run local nsys sweep — ETA 1 week for prototype.
- Hannah + Evan: run ncu parameter sweep for attention kernel launch configs and submit results into confluence playbook — ETA 3 weeks.

Appendix (quick trace excerpts):
- Example NVTX timeline snippet (translated): [host] enqueue request -> memcpyH2D (0.6ms) -> kernel(attention_fwd) (18.2ms) -> kernel(matmul_proj) (4.1ms) -> memcpyD2H (0.9ms) -> host-complete. When CUDA Graphs enabled the enqueue->kernel gaps disappear and host overhead goes from ~26ms -> ~8ms.
- Short heuristics: If p99 > 3x p95 and batch<=2 => likely kernel launch / scheduling or tiny-kernel low occupancy issue. If p99 ~ p95 and DRAM throughput >= 70% => memory-bandwidth saturation.

If you want, I can extract a CSV summarizing per-batch metrics (p50/p95/p99, achieved_occupancy for top 6 kernels, mem throughput) so we can attach it to the ticket and the playbook.
